context.text: Ignatius, called Theophoros, 'God-bearer', was the second bishop of Antioch after the apostles, in the church where the disciples were first called Christians. Under Trajan, being a Christian was itself a capital offense when pressed, and Ignatius was condemned to the beasts at Rome.

narrative.text: Escorted across Asia Minor by a squad of soldiers he called his 'ten leopards,' Ignatius was met at every city by the local churches. From Smyrna and Troas he wrote seven letters, to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia, Smyrna, and to Polycarp, that are among the most precious documents of the generation after the apostles.

The letters show, within eighty years of the Resurrection, a Church recognizably Orthodox: one bishop with presbyters and deacons in each city; the Eucharist as 'the medicine of immortality,' truly the flesh of Christ; and the church of Rome addressed as 'presiding in love.' To the Romans he begged that no one hinder his death: 'I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.' He was killed in the arena at Rome, by tradition around 107–110.

significance.text: Ignatius is the earliest witness after the New Testament to episcopal order and eucharistic realism, the claim that Orthodox faith and order are apostolic rests heavily on him. His word for the Church, 'katholike', catholic, whole, appears here for the first time in surviving literature.

uncertainty: The seven authentic letters are secure; the traditional date of his death under Trajan (c. 107–110) rests on Eusebius's chronology and cannot be independently verified.
